posts.quote: I'M THE ONLY ONE WHO KNOWS THE GRAVY RECIPE. THAT'S NOT A RESPONSIBILITY, IT'S A HOSTAGE SITUATION.
posts.caption: Every year somebody says the gravy tastes the way it always does. It's the nicest thing anyone says about my cooking, and it's also a warning. My mother wrote the recipe on the inside of a cabinet door in pencil, then painted the cabinet. So now it lives in my head and in one stained spoon. Last year I tried explaining the steps to my sister. I got as far as "until it looks right" and she went to check on something. I'm not mad. I'd have left too. The spoon stays with me.
posts.first: I made a test batch earlier this week to make sure I still had it. I did. Then I ate all of it standing at the stove with the spoon, so I'll be making it again anyway. This time with witnesses.

posts.quote: I SAID I'D SEND CHRISTMAS CARDS EARLY THIS YEAR. I FOUND A FULL BOX FROM 2019 AND FELT SOMETHING LIKE PRIDE.
posts.caption: There was a plan this year to do the cards early. A real plan, with stamps bought in September and a short note I'd already written in the shower. The box I found had eleven cards left, a pen that doesn't work, and a roll of stamps with a flag they've since redesigned. I stood in the hallway reading the verse inside, which is very confident about peace on earth. I'll probably send them anyway. The stamps may need a little help from their cousins.
posts.first: I used to think people who sent cards early were showing off. Now I think they're the ones who wrote down where the stamps went. Mine were in a drawer with the batteries, next to a tape measure I've also been looking for.

posts.quote: I SET MY WARM SOCKS ON THE RADIATOR AT 2 P.M. I'M NOT SAYING I'M LOOKING FORWARD TO BEDTIME, BUT I'VE BEEN THINKING ABOUT IT SINCE LUNCH.
posts.caption: The best thing I've figured out all fall costs nothing and takes four minutes. You set a pair of thick socks on the radiator in the afternoon, then go about your day and don't think about them. By bedtime they've become the nicest thing that has ever happened to your feet. I've started planning the evening around that moment. Dinner is a formality. The dishes are a rumor. The socks are the reason I'm getting into bed on time.
posts.first: My feet used to be cold from October until about May and I just lived like that. Then the radiator in the back room started working. That was a big year for me.

posts.quote: EVERYBODY IN THE STORE IS BUYING BUTTER. WE'RE ALL HAVING THE SAME HOLIDAY AND NONE OF US ARE OKAY.
posts.caption: I went in for one stick. That's the part I keep repeating to myself in the parking lot. There were six of us at the dairy case, all in coats, all reaching for the same shelf with the focus of people defusing something. A woman next to me said she needed twelve pounds. I asked what for. She said, a lot of people. I took four and quietly put one back. It seemed like what a decent person would do, and I wanted to be one for at least the length of that aisle.
posts.first: I made it to the register with two sticks and a feeling of having survived. The cashier said she'd sold forty-one pounds since morning. She said it like a weather report. I said it sounded about right.

posts.quote: I'VE WATCHED THE SAME COOKING SHOW FOR FOUR WEEKS TO PREPARE FOR THANKSGIVING. THE ONLY THING I'VE LEARNED IS HOW TO SAY "FOLD IN GENTLY."
posts.caption: I've been watching a baking show for about a month, and I'd like it noted that I haven't baked a single thing. There's a man on it who can make a pie crust look like a hobby, and he never raises his voice, even when somebody ruins a custard. I find that very relaxing. Thanksgiving will be store-bought rolls and my own confidence, but I'll know the vocabulary. When someone asks if I proofed something, I'll nod and say overnight.
posts.first: A man on the show said to let the dough tell you when it's ready. I let mine tell me. It said nothing, and I took that as a yes.

posts.quote: THE HEAT CAME ON TODAY AND THE WHOLE HOUSE SMELLED LIKE BURNING DUST. I CALLED IT "FIREPLACE AMBIANCE" AND KEPT WALKING.
posts.caption: Every year the first cold day follows the same sequence. The vent clicks, a warm smell rolls out like somebody opened an old drawer, and I stand in the hallway with the emotional range of someone who's just been lied to by a candle. It lasts about an hour. By then the house has burned off the dust of the whole summer and settled back down. I wipe the top of the bookcase so I feel like I did something. I didn't. I just moved it.
posts.first: My neighbor says her house smells like cinnamon when the heat comes on. Mine smells like the inside of a vacuum. We both said cozy and let it go.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a grey-streaked messy bun and a pencil in it standing in a hallway beside a heating vent with dust drifting up, waving a hand in front of her nose with a deadpan look, a glass of red wine in her other hand. posts.caption: I don't read fast on purpose. When it's a good one, I read in small bites so there's always a few chapters left to look forward to. Nobody's rushing me.
posts.first: I've been on the same novel since the middle of October. The bookmark is a grocery receipt and it's getting a little brave. I think we're both fine with the arrangement.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a plump woman with short mauve-pink curls curled up in an armchair in a reading nook, holding an open book with her thumb in the back pages and a wistful expression, a mug of tea beside her. Text in a speech bubble reads: I started a new book and loved it. I'm already checking how many pages are left. I'm not ready for us to be over.
